```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5
)
has_decido <- requireNamespace("decido", quietly = TRUE)
has_rtriangle <- requireNamespace("RTriangle", quietly = TRUE)
has_cdtr <- requireNamespace("cdtr", quietly = TRUE)
has_silicate <- requireNamespace("silicate", quietly = TRUE)
```

A polygon in wkpool is a set of rings, and a ring is a cycle of segments:
one-dimensional topology. Triangles are the two-dimensional version, and
they can live on the same vertex pool. A `wkpool_tri` is a vector of
triangles whose corners are vertex ids into a pool, just as a wkpool is a
vector of segments.

`wkpool_tri` and `pool_triangulate()` are **experimental** (new in 0.4.0)
and may change. The older route, `as_pslg()` and `pool_holes()` feeding
RTriangle, is unchanged and is covered below alongside the newer engines.

```{r setup}
library(wkpool)
```

## Ear cutting

`pool_triangulate()` ear cuts each polygon with decido. Ear cutting adds
no vertices, so the triangles reference the pool's vertices as they are.

```{r earcut, eval = has_decido}
x <- wk::as_wkb(c(
  "POLYGON ((0 0, 4 0, 4 4, 0 4, 0 0), (1 1, 1 3, 2 2, 3 3, 3 1, 1 1))",
  "POLYGON ((4 0, 6 0, 6 4, 4 4, 4 0))"
))
pool <- establish_topology(x)
tri <- pool_triangulate(pool)
tri
pool_triangles(tri)
```

```{r earcut-plot, eval = has_decido, fig.height = 4}
plot(tri, asp = 1)
```

Each triangle keeps the feature and part it came from, and triangles are
counter-clockwise. `wk_handle()` gives one POLYGON per triangle, so any wk
consumer can take them:

```{r earcut-wk, eval = has_decido}
wk::as_wkt(tri)[1:3]
```

Triangulating a raw pool and merging later gives the same result as
merging first. After merging, the two features share the corners on their
common edge. `tri_segments()` gives the triangle edges as an ordinary
wkpool, so the segment tools apply; here the one edge the features share,
once from each side:

```{r earcut-merge, eval = has_decido}
tri <- merge_coincident(tri)
edges <- tri_segments(tri)
find_shared_edges(edges)
```

## A real coverage

`inlandwaters` from silicate is six regions of Australia (and New
Caledonia) with many holes and long shared boundaries.

```{r inlandwaters, eval = has_decido && has_silicate, message = FALSE}
data("inlandwaters", package = "silicate")
iw <- merge_coincident(establish_topology(inlandwaters))
iw_tri <- pool_triangulate(iw)
length(iw_tri)
nrow(pool_vertices(iw_tri)) == nrow(pool_vertices(iw))
plot(iw_tri, border = NA, asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
```

`plot()` draws every triangle in one `polygon()` call indexed into the
pool, so tens of thousands of triangles draw in well under a second.

## Constrained Delaunay: the PSLG route

Ear cutting gives valid triangles but they are often long and thin, and
it cannot add vertices. For good-quality triangles (minimum angle, maximum
area) you need a constrained Delaunay triangulation, and its input is a
planar straight line graph (PSLG): vertices, and segments that must appear
as triangle edges. A merged pool is already a PSLG; `as_pslg()` just
gives it as matrices, `P` for the vertices and `S` for the segments, in
the form RTriangle uses.

```{r pslg}
p <- as_pslg(establish_topology(wk::as_wkb(
  "POLYGON ((0 0, 4 0, 4 4, 0 4, 0 0), (1 1, 1 3, 2 2, 3 3, 3 1, 1 1))"
)))
str(p)
```

A PSLG does not say which side of a segment is inside. RTriangle removes
the triangles outside the outer boundary, and needs a point in each hole
to remove those too. `pool_holes()` gives one point inside each hole ring
(a hole that another polygon fills exactly, like an enclave, is not a
hole of the coverage and is left out):

```{r rtriangle, eval = has_rtriangle, fig.height = 4}
h <- pool_holes(merge_coincident(establish_topology(wk::as_wkb(
  "POLYGON ((0 0, 4 0, 4 4, 0 4, 0 0), (1 1, 1 3, 2 2, 3 3, 3 1, 1 1))"
))))
h
rt <- RTriangle::triangulate(RTriangle::pslg(P = p$P, S = p$S, H = h),
                             q = 30, a = 0.1)
plot(rt$P, asp = 1, pch = ".", xlab = "", ylab = "")
polygon(rt$P[t(cbind(rt$T, NA)), ], col = "grey90")
points(h, col = "firebrick", pch = 19)
```

RTriangle added vertices to meet the quality and area targets; those are
the Steiner points, appended after the input vertices.

cdtr is a newer constrained Delaunay engine for R that takes the same
inputs. It counts how many boundaries each triangle sits inside (its
depth), so with `erase = "holes"` it needs no hole points at all:

```{r cdtr, eval = has_cdtr, fig.height = 4}
cd <- cdtr::cdt_pslg(p, erase = "holes", min_angle = 30, max_area = 0.1)
table(cd$origin)
plot(cd$P, asp = 1, pch = ".", xlab = "", ylab = "")
polygon(cd$P[t(cbind(cd$T, NA)), ], col = "grey90")
```

## Back to a triangle pool

The result of either engine is a vertex table and an index table, which
is all a `wkpool_tri` is. The input vertices come first in the same order
as the pool, so their ids are unchanged and Steiner points get new ids
after them:

```{r back, eval = has_cdtr}
v <- data.frame(.vx = seq_len(nrow(cd$P)), x = cd$P[, 1], y = cd$P[, 2])
cd_tri <- new_wkpool_tri(v, cd$T[, 1], cd$T[, 2], cd$T[, 3])
length(cd_tri)
cd_tri[1:3]
```

On real data the difference in triangle quality is plain. The first
feature of `inlandwaters` is the Australian Capital Territory: ear cut on
the left, long thin triangles fanning from a few vertices; through cdtr
with a minimum angle of 25 degrees on the right, back on a triangle pool:

```{r act-cdt, eval = has_cdtr && has_decido && has_silicate, message = FALSE}
act <- iw_tri[pool_feature(iw_tri) == 1]
act_p <- as_pslg(establish_topology(inlandwaters[1, ]))
act_cd <- cdtr::cdt_pslg(act_p, min_angle = 25)
act_v <- data.frame(.vx = seq_len(nrow(act_cd$P)),
                    x = act_cd$P[, 1], y = act_cd$P[, 2])
act_cdt <- new_wkpool_tri(act_v, act_cd$T[, 1], act_cd$T[, 2], act_cd$T[, 3])
c(earcut = length(act), cdtr = length(act_cdt))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = rep(0.5, 4))
plot(act, col = "grey90", border = "grey40", asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "")
plot(act_cdt, col = "grey90", border = "grey40", asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "")
par(op)
```

The PSLG route triangulates the whole pool at once and does not record
which feature a triangle belongs to; `pool_triangulate()` does, because it
works one polygon at a time.

On `inlandwaters` both engines cover the same area as ear cutting, up to
one thing a PSLG cannot express without help: a region enclosed by
neighbouring polygons that none of them covers is not a hole of any ring,
so `pool_holes()` gives no point for it and RTriangle keeps it. cdtr's
depth sees it as outside.

```{r compare, eval = has_rtriangle && has_cdtr && has_decido && has_silicate}
tri_area <- function(P, T) {
  sum(abs((P[T[, 2], 1] - P[T[, 1], 1]) * (P[T[, 3], 2] - P[T[, 1], 2]) -
          (P[T[, 3], 1] - P[T[, 1], 1]) * (P[T[, 2], 2] - P[T[, 1], 2]))) / 2
}
iw_p <- as_pslg(iw)
iw_rt <- RTriangle::triangulate(
  RTriangle::pslg(P = iw_p$P, S = iw_p$S, H = pool_holes(iw))
)
iw_cd <- cdtr::cdt_pslg(iw_p, erase = "holes")
ev <- pool_vertices(iw_tri)
c(
  earcut = tri_area(cbind(ev$x, ev$y), as.matrix(pool_triangles(iw_tri)[1:3])),
  RTriangle = tri_area(iw_rt$P, iw_rt$T),
  cdtr = tri_area(iw_cd$P, iw_cd$T)
) / 1e6
```

## Which engine

| Engine | Adds vertices | Keeps feature | Holes from | Status |
|--------|---------------|---------------|------------|--------|
| `pool_triangulate()` (decido) | no | yes | ring roles | experimental, in wkpool |
| RTriangle via `as_pslg()` | yes (quality, area) | no | `pool_holes()` points | CRAN, non-free licence |
| cdtr via `as_pslg()` | yes (quality, area) | no | depth | MIT |

[meshcore](https://github.com/hypertidy/meshcore) wraps cdtr and laridae
(CGAL) behind `tri_mesh()` and returns the triangles in its mesh table
form, with vertex origin (input, crossing, Steiner) and depth recorded.
